On 12 June 2026, the American company Anthropic switched off worldwide access to two of its newest artificial-intelligence models, Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5, after the US Department of Commerce imposed export controls on them. The order barred use by foreign nationals and extended even to the company’s own foreign employees. Eighteen days later, on 30 June, Commerce lifted the controls, and access was restored on 1 July. Commerce said it had worked with the company to analyse and approve the models, and the company reported that a government testing body had judged its revised safeguards very strong. The episode lasted less than three weeks, but it is a useful case study, because it exposed a question that regulators have so far avoided: what does it mean to “export” a piece of software that anyone with an internet connection can reach?

Traditional export controls were designed for objects. A centrifuge, a guidance chip or a tank crosses a border at a customs post, where it can be inspected, licensed or stopped. Controls on technology have always been harder, because knowledge moves in heads and on disks, but even there the transaction was identifiable: a firm sold a design or a manual to a named buyer. A frontier model accessed through a web interface is neither. Nothing physically leaves the country; a query travels to a server, and an answer travels back. To control such a service, the state must regulate not the shipment but the access, which in practice means regulating the company’s customers and, as the June order showed, its own staff. The doctrine of “deemed export”, under which releasing controlled technology to a foreign national inside the United States counts as an export to that person’s country, is what makes such a reach possible.

The stated justification was national security. Fable is a version of the company’s most capable model, Mythos, with additional safeguards intended to make it suitable for the public; Mythos itself, whose abilities in finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities are especially strong, had been confined to vetted organisations under a limited-access programme meant mainly for cyber-defence. The regulator’s worry, as reported, was that the safeguards separating the two could be circumvented. This is the dual-use problem in its purest form. The same capability that lets a defender locate a flaw in a hospital’s software before criminals do lets an attacker locate it first, and no inspection of the model can separate the benign use from the malicious one, because they are the same use. Restriction therefore falls on defenders and attackers alike. Critics noted precisely this, observing that those most hurt by the ban were organisations that needed to test their own systems.

Defenders of the order offer three arguments. The first is precaution: where the downside is a large-scale attack on infrastructure, it is rational to act before the evidence is conclusive, since an irreversible harm cannot be compensated afterwards. The second concerns leverage. A government that waits for a firm to volunteer safeguards has little bargaining power; a government that can switch off a product has a great deal, and the negotiation that followed produced testing of the safeguards by a federal evaluator and a set of access conditions. The third is jurisdictional: a rule that binds only firms willing to be bound is not a rule, and export law is an instrument the executive already holds that reaches software developers without new legislation.

Each argument has a weak point. Precaution cuts both ways, because withdrawing a tool from defenders is itself a risk, and a standard that demands proof of safety before release is one that no sufficiently capable system can meet, since safety against determined misuse is not something a model can demonstrate in advance. Leverage exercised through an abrupt order, with its reasoning unexplained, teaches firms to anticipate and avoid the regulator rather than to cooperate with it; observers remarked that the lack of clarity about what made these models uniquely risky has shaped how other developers approach their own releases. And reliance on a statute written for physical goods and for a cold-war style of rivalry, instead of on rules debated and enacted for the purpose, means that the criteria for a ban remain in the hands of officials and may change with the administration.

There is also the question of who bears the cost of uncertainty. For a large American firm, eighteen days without revenue from two products is survivable. For a company in Bengaluru or Lagos that had built a product on top of the models, the interruption could be existential, and it had no standing to appeal to the American authority that caused it. This asymmetry, one jurisdiction deciding and many absorbing the consequences, is a recurring feature of technology governance, and it helps explain why governments outside the United States, India’s among them, have shown interest in domestic capacity: not because they expect to match the leading laboratories, but because dependence on a foreign supplier who can be ordered to cut service is itself a strategic exposure.

What, then, did the episode settle? Less than either camp claims. It did not show that the controls were wise. The models were cleared after under three weeks without, so far as is publicly known, any incident having occurred, which proponents read as proof that the pause worked and critics as proof that it was unnecessary. Both readings are consistent with the facts, and that is the difficulty: a precaution that succeeds is indistinguishable from an overreaction that was never needed. Nor did it settle the legal question. Lifting an order is not the same as defining a standard, and the next frontier release will meet the same ambiguity unless the criteria are written down in advance.

The more durable lesson concerns the form of regulation rather than its target. A regime that works through sudden prohibition produces a particular kind of firm behaviour: lobbying, secrecy and a premium on political access. A regime that publishes thresholds, specifies the tests a model must pass, and commits in advance to the process of review would be slower to arrive but easier to live with, and would give those who build on these systems, far from Washington, something on which to base their plans.
questions.question: The author’s main purpose in the passage is
options: A) to argue that the June order was an unjustified intrusion by the state into a private firm’s freedom to sell its software to customers in other countries
B) to defend the order as a necessary precaution against attacks that the firm’s own safeguards had already failed to prevent in actual practice
C) to use one episode to show how export law strains when applied to software services, and why rules should be set in advance
D) to predict that other governments will soon copy the American order and impose similar limits on technology firms based inside their own borders
questions.explanation: Explanation: The author treats the episode as a case study (para 1), shows how export concepts built for objects strain (para 2), and ends by urging published rules (final para). The author neither condemns nor defends the order outright, and makes no prediction about other governments.

questions.question: Which of the following, if true, would most weaken the author’s claim that a successful precaution “is indistinguishable from an overreaction that was never needed”?
options: A) Several rival firms released models of comparable ability during the same eighteen days without any resulting harm being reported to the authorities.
B) Government witnesses admitted that no formal assessment of the models’ ability to find software flaws had been completed before the order was issued.
C) Companies that had built products on the models reported losses far larger than the American government had estimated before issuing the order.
D) Monitoring showed that attempts to bypass the safeguards would have succeeded had access continued.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Para 7: the claim is that the lack of an incident cannot separate the two readings. Evidence that bypass attempts would actually have worked is evidence only the ‘precaution’ reading predicts, so the readings become distinguishable. The other options bear on harm elsewhere, process or cost, not on this inference.

A patent grants a temporary monopoly, which lets the inventor charge more than the cost of production and so recoup the expense of discovery. The price is paid by consumers, who face higher prices during the monopoly, and the monopoly itself discourages use: some who would have benefited from the product at a price near its cost are priced out. A prize can reward only what its designers could imagine beforehand, and what proves most valuable in invention is often the thing nobody expected.

A patent grants a temporary monopoly, which lets the inventor charge more than the cost of production and so recoup the expense of discovery. The price is paid by consumers, who face higher prices during the monopoly, and the monopoly itself discourages use: some who would have benefited from the product at a price near its cost are priced out. This deadweight loss is the central cost of the system, and it is felt most sharply in medicine, where a patented drug may be unaffordable to those who need it. The instrument is also a rough one, since the length of the monopoly is fixed by law rather than by the value of the invention, so that a trivial improvement and a transformative discovery may be granted the same term.

A prize avoids this cost. If the state or a philanthropist pays a sum for the invention and then places it in the public domain, the invention can be produced competitively at cost. The monopoly disappears and the incentive survives. Advocates point to advance market commitments for vaccines, in which donors promise to buy a fixed quantity at an agreed price if a product meeting specified criteria is developed, as a case where the logic has been applied. A further attraction is that prizes can be directed at needs that the market neglects: diseases of the poor, which offer no profitable monopoly because the patients cannot pay. Prizes also have a long record outside medicine: aviation prizes in the early twentieth century drew competitors to long-distance flight, and modern competitions in machine learning and clean-energy engineering have attracted teams that no grant committee would have thought to fund. A prize pays only for success, so the sponsor bears no cost for the many attempts that fail.

The difficulty lies in the size and the setting of the prize. A patent’s reward is determined by the market: the invention that consumers value most earns the most, and nobody need be told in advance what it is worth. A prize must be fixed by someone, in advance and without knowing the value of the thing to be discovered. If it is set too low, nobody bothers to compete; if too high, public money is wasted. The sponsor must also specify what counts as success. This is easy when the goal is crisp, like crossing an ocean or sequencing a genome, and hard when the goal is ill-defined or a matter of degree, as with a better teaching method. A prize can reward only what its designers could imagine beforehand, and what proves most valuable in invention is often the thing nobody expected.

The longitude prize is, in this light, a less clean example than it appears. Harrison’s clocks met the test of accuracy, but the board assessing the prize, which included astronomers committed to a rival method based on lunar observations, disputed his claim for years, and he received the bulk of the sum only after appealing to the king. This is evidence that prizes are vulnerable to the interests and biases of those who judge them. It is also true that the instrument that eventually dominated was not Harrison’s costly original but a cheaper chronometer developed by later makers, and the prize had little to do with its spread, which was driven by the market for ships’ instruments. The prize may have been more useful in focusing attention on the problem than in rewarding its solution.

Most economists now see the question as one of fit rather than rivalry. Patents suit settings where the value of an invention is uncertain and spread across many users, and where the inventor can find a market. Prizes suit settings where the goal is clear, the beneficiaries cannot pay, or the monopoly cost is intolerable. Grants for research, which pay for effort rather than results, suit early-stage work where success cannot be specified in advance and failures teach something. A third family of arrangements, in which patents are bought out by the state and released for general use, tries to combine the market’s discovery of value with the prize’s removal of monopoly pricing, though it requires a valuation of the patent, and so inherits the prize’s central problem.

What this debate shows is that incentives for invention cannot be assessed solely by whether they produce more invention. A system that generates a great deal of research on trivial improvements for those who can pay, and none on conditions that afflict the poor, is productive in one sense and defective in another. The question for policy is therefore not which instrument is best in general but which problems are being solved, for whom, and at what cost in access. Seen this way, the choice among patents, prizes and grants is a choice about what a society wishes to see invented, and whom it intends to benefit, and no instrument settles that question in advance.
questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the author’s conclusion?
options: A) No single instrument is best; the choice reflects what a society wants invented and for whom
B) Prizes are superior to patents wherever the monopoly cost is high, and patents remain superior wherever a market for the invention exists
C) Incentive systems should be judged by the volume of invention that they produce, since access is a matter for separate and later policy
D) Grants are the best of the three instruments, because they reward effort rather than results and so avoid the problems of valuation
questions.explanation: Explanation: Final paragraph: the choice among patents, prizes and grants is a choice about what a society wishes to see invented and whom it intends to benefit. The author explicitly rejects judging by volume of invention alone.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Yet the longer a firm survives, the more its routines harden into rules that nobody remembers choosing.
2. Routines are valuable because they let an organisation act without deliberating over every decision.
3. This rigidity becomes costly when the environment changes and the old routines no longer fit.
4. Studies of long-lived firms therefore stress the capacity to revise routines as much as the capacity to follow them.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 introduces routines and their value, 1 (‘Yet’) turns to the downside, 3 (‘This rigidity’) states the cost, and 4 (‘therefore’) draws the conclusion.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Only when he gave up the circle altogether did the figures fall into place.
2. For centuries astronomers had assumed that planets travel in circles, the most perfect of shapes.
3. Kepler, working on the orbit of Mars, found that no circle could be fitted to the data without a small but persistent error.
4. The ellipse he adopted instead became the first of his three laws of planetary motion.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 gives the old assumption, 3 the anomaly, 1 (‘Only when he gave up the circle’) the break, and 4 (‘The ellipse he adopted instead’) the outcome.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. A tax on carbon raises the price of fossil fuels and so gives consumers a reason to use less of them.
2. Critics respond that the poor spend a larger share of their income on energy, so the burden falls unevenly.
3. Many economists therefore propose returning the revenue to households as equal dividends.
4. Supporters regard it as the most efficient way to cut emissions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 1 describes the tax, 4 (‘it’) gives its supporters’ view, 2 the critics’ objection, and 3 (‘therefore’) the proposed remedy.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. Memory, on this view, is not a recording but a reconstruction.
2. Each time a memory is recalled, it is rebuilt from fragments and may be altered by what has happened since.
3. Witnesses can therefore be entirely sincere and yet wrong.
4. Psychologists who study testimony have shown that confident recollections are often inaccurate.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 4 states the finding, 1 (‘on this view’) the explanation, 2 the mechanism, and 3 (‘therefore’) the implication for witnesses.

questions.question:
Rearrange the four sentences (1-4) into a logical sequence (Type the 4-digit sequence as answer):

1. The result was a boom in lending that ended when borrowers could no longer repay.
2. When interest rates fell sharply, borrowing became cheap and investors searched for higher returns.
3. Some of them found these in assets that appeared safe but carried risks hidden in their structure.
4. Banks, eager to meet the demand, expanded credit to borrowers with weak records.
questions.explanation: Explanation: 2 sets the cause, 3 (‘Some of them’, ‘these’) continues with investors, 4 brings in the banks, and 1 (‘The result’) gives the outcome.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'During the Second World War, analysts examining bombers that returned from missions noted where the bullet holes clustered and proposed reinforcing those areas. The statistician Abraham Wald objected that the sample consisted only of aircraft that had survived; the places with few holes were precisely those where a hit proved fatal. The case shows how the evidence that reaches us is filtered by what it takes to be observed, so that what is missing may be more informative than what is visible.'
options: A) Evidence is filtered by survival, so what is absent from a sample may matter more than what is present.
B) Bombers should be reinforced where bullet holes are fewest, because those areas have been shown by wartime statistics to be the ones most often struck.
C) Wald showed that military analysts of the period were generally careless, since they relied on samples that were too small to support any firm conclusion.
D) Damage patterns on returning aircraft give a reliable guide to where armour is needed, provided the number of aircraft examined is large enough.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph’s point is survivorship bias: missing observations can be more informative. The distractors misstate Wald’s reasoning or turn on sample size.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'The longer a non-perishable thing such as a book or a technology has survived, the longer its likely remaining life, a regularity sometimes called the Lindy effect. The logic is that survival is itself evidence of robustness. The rule does not apply to perishables such as people, whose expected remaining life shortens with age, and it can mislead where survival has been secured by protection rather than merit.'
options: A) Anything that has lasted a long time must be of high quality, because only the best books and technologies are able to survive over the years.
B) Survival signals robustness in non-perishables, but the inference fails for perishables and for protected survivors.
C) Older people can expect to live longer than younger people, in the same way that an old book can expect to outlast one that is recent.
D) The Lindy effect is a myth, since the survival of an object over a long period tells us nothing about how long it is likely to continue.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph states a rule, its logic and two limits. The distractors drop the limits or reverse the claim.

questions.question:
Select the option that best summarizes the paragraph:

'In 1865 William Stanley Jevons noted that improvements in the efficiency of steam engines, far from reducing coal consumption, increased it, as cheaper power found new uses. Modern analysts find that efficiency gains can likewise be eroded by rebound effects, though the size varies: for goods such as home heating, where demand is close to saturation, most of the saving is retained, while for goods such as computing, use expands greatly.'
options: A) Efficiency improvements always increase total consumption of the resource, as Jevons showed, and so policies that promote efficiency should be abandoned.
B) Home heating and computing differ in cost, and the difference in cost explains why efficiency has reduced coal consumption in one but not in the other.
C) Efficiency gains can be partly or wholly offset by greater use, to an extent that depends on how saturated demand is.
D) Modern analysts have refuted Jevons by showing that efficiency gains are retained in full for almost every good that people use in daily life.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The paragraph says rebound effects vary with saturation. ‘Always’, ‘cost’ and ‘refuted’ are not supported.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'Economists distinguish between a fall in the price level and a fall in the rate of inflation. The latter, called disinflation, means that prices are still rising, only more slowly. Deflation means that the price level itself is falling. The distinction matters because deflation raises the real burden of fixed nominal debts, whereas disinflation ________.'
options: A) merely slows the rate at which rising prices erode that burden
B) raises the burden in the same manner as deflation, because both reduce the growth of prices in the economy as a whole
C) has no effect on debtors, since they are free to renegotiate their loans whenever the rate of inflation begins to fall
D) lowers the burden even faster than inflation does, because prices are rising by smaller amounts than in earlier years
questions.explanation: Explanation: Under disinflation prices still rise, so inflation still erodes the real value of debt, only more slowly. The distractors equate it with deflation, ignore debt, or reverse the effect.

questions.question:
Complete the paragraph logically:

'A dominant strategy in game theory is one that yields the best outcome whatever the other players do. In the prisoner’s dilemma, confessing is dominant for each prisoner, and yet when both confess they do worse than if both had stayed silent. The dilemma thus shows that ________.'
options: A) a dominant strategy is only rational when every other player has already announced which strategy he or she intends to follow
B) individually rational choices can combine into a collectively worse outcome
C) prisoners who are allowed to communicate will always choose silence, since silence is better for both of them taken together
D) the best outcome for a group is always reached when each member ignores the others and looks only to his or her own interest
questions.explanation: Explanation: Each prisoner’s dominant choice leaves both worse off than mutual silence. The distractors misdefine dominance, assert communication outcomes, or claim self-interest always serves the group.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'PERSPICACIOUS':
options: A) Astute
B) Obtuse
C) Garrulous
D) Imperious
questions.explanation: Explanation: Perspicacious means having keen insight; ‘astute’ is closest. ‘Obtuse’ is the opposite.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'EPHEMERAL':
options: A) Evanescent
B) Fleeting
C) Perpetual
D) Brief
questions.explanation: Explanation: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time; ‘perpetual’ is the antonym. The others are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY SIMILAR in meaning to 'OBSEQUIOUS':
options: A) Imperious
B) Candid
C) Truculent
D) Servile
questions.explanation: Explanation: Obsequious means excessively eager to please or obey; ‘servile’ matches. ‘Imperious’ is its opposite in manner.

questions.question: Select the word MOST NEARLY OPPOSITE in meaning to 'PRODIGAL':
options: A) Profligate
B) Thrifty
C) Extravagant
D) Lavish
questions.explanation: Explanation: Prodigal means wastefully extravagant; ‘thrifty’ is the antonym.

questions.question:
Choose the correct word to fill in the blank:
'The editor praised the report for its ________ style, in which not a single word was wasted.'
options: A) prolix
B) terse
C) ornate
D) bombastic
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Terse’ means brief and to the point. The others suggest wordiness or ornament.

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills the blanks:
'Although the ________ of the scheme was widely conceded, the committee remained ________ about funding it.'
options: A) merit; sceptical
B) folly; unwilling
C) novelty; enthusiastic
D) expense; delighted
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Although’ signals contrast: admitted merit set against doubt about funding. In the other pairs the second word does not contrast with the first.

questions.question:
Choose the correct idiom meaning:
'To throw down the gauntlet' means to:
options: A) concede defeat before a contest has properly begun
B) issue a challenge
C) seek forgiveness publicly for an earlier insult
D) protect oneself with armour before a fight starts
questions.explanation: Explanation: In the age of chivalry, throwing down a gauntlet was a formal challenge to combat.

questions.question: Select the sentence in which the word 'DISINTERESTED' is used correctly (in its standard sense):
options: A) The judge was disinterested in the lecture and yawned throughout it.
B) She felt disinterested in the novel after its first chapters had bored her.
C) A disinterested referee is trusted by both sides.
D) He gave a disinterested shrug when asked about the football results.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Standard sense: impartial, with no stake in the outcome. In the other sentences it is misused for ‘uninterested’.

questions.question: Select the option that best gives the meaning of 'PERFUNCTORY':
options: A) performed with great care and attention to every small detail involved
B) said in a manner intended to hurt or to offend the listener present
C) based on guesswork rather than on any firm evidence that was available
D) done as a routine, without real interest
questions.explanation: Explanation: Perfunctory means carried out with minimal effort or interest.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'Neither the coach nor the players ________ satisfied with the result.'
options: A) was
B) were
C) has been
D) is
questions.explanation: Explanation: With ‘neither… nor’, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, ‘players’ (plural); the past context needs ‘were’.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'The number of applicants (A) / for the scholarship (B) / have increased (C) / this year (D).'
options: A) The number of applicants
B) for the scholarship
C) have increased
D) this year
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘The number of’ takes a singular verb: ‘has increased’. (‘A number of’ would take a plural.)

questions.question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
options: A) The reason he failed is because he did not study enough for the examination.
B) He is one of those students who always do their homework.
C) Between you and I, the plan will fail unless the committee changes its mind.
D) Each of the proposed plans have flaws that the committee has not yet noticed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In ‘one of those students who…’ the verb agrees with ‘students’. The others contain ‘reason… is because’, ‘between you and I’ and ‘each… have’.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'I wish you ________ the truth when I asked you yesterday.'
options: A) told
B) have told
C) had told
D) would tell
questions.explanation: Explanation: A wish about the past takes the past perfect.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'The economist ________ theory the minister cited has since revised it.'
options: A) who
B) whom
C) whose
D) of which
questions.explanation: Explanation: The possessive relative ‘whose’ is required before ‘theory’.

questions.question:
Spot the error in the sentence:
'He is not only (A) / a gifted musician (B) / but also (C) / writes poetry (D).'
options: A) He is not only
B) a gifted musician
C) but also
D) writes poetry
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Not only… but also’ must join parallel structures: ‘a gifted musician but also a poet’.

questions.question:
Choose the correct option to fill in the blank:
'If I ________ you, I would accept the offer.'
options: A) was
B) am
C) would be
D) were
questions.explanation: Explanation: The subjunctive ‘were’ is used in unreal present conditions.

questions.question: Identify the grammatically INCORRECT sentence:
options: A) She insisted on paying the bill after the long dinner with colleagues.
B) I look forward to meeting you at the conference next month in Delhi.
C) He is accustomed to work late into the night.
D) They had hardly begun the match when heavy rain started to fall.
questions.explanation: Explanation: ‘Accustomed to’ takes a gerund: ‘accustomed to working’.
